title: [Issue] docs(ingestion): concurrency tuning guide + warning for the sequential per-file ingest() pattern
description:
# Ingestion concurrency: better defaults, tuning guide, and a warning for the per-file ingest() loop pattern

## Problem

Two related pitfalls make first-run ingestion look much slower than the SDK actually is:

1. **Conservative defaults.** `ingest()` batches at `max_concurrency=3` documents in flight (`src/graphrag_sdk/api/main.py:1579`) and the extractor defaults to 12 concurrent LLM calls (`ingestion/extraction_strategies/graph_extraction.py:523`). Reasonable for laptops against rate-limited APIs; far below what a local model server or enterprise API tier can sustain. Nothing tells the user these knobs exist.

2. **Silent zero-parallelism pattern.** Calling `ingest(source)` in a loop over files — the most natural-looking usage — gives zero document-level parallelism, with no warning. Passing the list in one call is what engages `_ingest_batch`'s semaphore. A POC evaluating the SDK this way concluded "PDF ingestion is a bottleneck" when it was running one document at a time.

## Proposed improvements

- **Docs: a tuning guide** — one page covering `max_concurrency`, extractor `max_concurrency`, `update_concurrency` (see #284), which stage dominates (LLM extraction for typical PDF workloads, not the graph write), and how to tell (per-step ctx logs already exist in `pipeline.run()`).
- **Runtime hint** — detect the sequential-single-source pattern (e.g. N single-source `ingest()` calls within one process/session) and log an INFO/WARNING pointing at list-based ingestion.
- **Revisit defaults** — consider raising the document default and/or deriving it from the model provider (local endpoints tolerate much more than metered APIs).

Related: #282/#283 fix the write path; this issue fixes the perception gap where extraction parallelism is left on the table.
 Labels: enhancement

title: [Issue] feat(ingestion): guardrail + normalization for relationship-type explosion in open-schema extraction
description:
# Guard against relationship-type explosion in open-schema extraction

## Problem

With no ontology, the extraction LLM invents relationship types freely. A production deployment ended up with **8,607 raw relationship types for ~25 canonical ones** (normalization existed only in their reporting layer, not before write).

This hurts twice:

1. **Server-side**: in FalkorDB every relationship type is a separate GraphBLAS matrix — 8.6K matrices is real memory overhead and degrades traversal/query planning. The SDK should protect the database from this.
2. **Client-side**: `upsert_relationships` groups by type (`storage/graph_store.py:157-162`), so noisy types fragment batches into thousands of tiny UNWIND queries — multiplying the round-trip problem tracked in #283.

## Proposed improvements

- **Warn** when distinct relationship-type cardinality grows pathologically (e.g. >100), at ingest time — today it's silent.
- **Optional write-time normalization** — a hook or built-in strategy that collapses raw types onto a canonical set before they hit the graph (case/tense/synonym folding at minimum; optionally embedding-based clustering).
- **Migration path** for existing graphs — a maintenance operation that rewrites edges from raw types onto canonical types (FalkorDB has no APOC; needs an explicit per-type rewrite query).

## Relationship to existing issues

Adjacent to #225 (finalize(): promote RELATES to typed edges) and #234 (emit typed edges at extraction time) — both *increase* exposure to this problem, since more typed edges means more opportunities for type sprawl. This issue is the guardrail/normalization layer they'd both need; cross-linking rather than merging.
 Labels: enhancement

title: [Issue] perf(update): make concurrent update() safe by design — update_concurrency=1 serializes incremental refreshes
description:
# Make concurrent update() safe so update_concurrency can be raised above 1

## Problem

`update()` defaults to `update_concurrency=1`, and the docstring is explicit: *"Default is 1, and you almost certainly should not raise it"* (`src/graphrag_sdk/api/main.py:2439`) — orphan cleanup is only correct under concurrent updates because of a fragile ordering invariant (MENTIONED_IN edges persisted before `run()` returns; see comments in `ingestion/pipeline.py:241-260`). Raising it risks wrongly deleting a shared entity when two concurrent updates both see it as an orphan candidate.

For update-heavy workloads this is the structural bottleneck: a production weekly refresh of ~18K modified documents runs fully serialized — **~55-hour ETA (≈3 days) for a weekly job**. Even with #282 and #283 landed, document-level serialization caps throughput at one document's pipeline latency per document.

## Fix direction

Make concurrent updates safe **by design** rather than by ordering invariant, so the default can be raised. Candidate approaches:

- **Entity-level locking** — serialize only updates that touch the same entity ids.
- **Partition-by-shared-entity scheduling** — pre-compute candidate entity overlap between modified docs; run non-overlapping partitions concurrently.
- **Harden the existing invariant** — make orphan-candidate checks transactional/recheck-before-delete so a concurrent writer cannot invalidate them between check and delete.

Whatever the approach, it must be designed against **`IncrementalResolution`** (the default resolver as of #278) — its graph-aware linking reads the live graph during resolution, so concurrency safety for orphan cleanup and for resolution reads should be solved together, not separately.

## Acceptance

- `update_concurrency > 1` documented as safe (and ideally a higher default).
- A concurrency stress test covering the shared-entity orphan race (extend `test_concurrent_updates_preserve_shared_entity`).

Related: #282, #283 (per-query costs; this issue is the parallelism ceiling above them).

title: [Issue] perf(ingestion): bulk write path for relationships — avoid per-doc per-type sequential UNWIND round trips
description:
# Bulk write path for relationships — per-doc per-type sequential round trips dominate ingestion

## Problem

Writes happen per document inside `pipeline.run()` (`src/graphrag_sdk/ingestion/pipeline.py:232-269`), and `upsert_relationships` groups by relationship type (`storage/graph_store.py:157-162`). Consequences:

- A document touching 25-30 relationship types pays **25-30 sequential UNWIND round trips**, each nearly empty.
- The 500-row `_BATCH_SIZE` batching effectively never engages — per-doc per-type groups are far smaller than 500.
- Per-label node upserts, relationship upserts, and mentions writes are all sequential `await`s.

Measured in a production incremental-update workload (~18K docs): **~20 min per 100-doc batch, dominated by ~25-30 UNWIND queries × network latency**. An SDK user asked directly: *"Does the GraphRAG SDK have a bulk write path for edge insertion that avoids per-type-per-batch round trips?"* — today the answer is no.

## Fix — two stages

**Stage 1 (cheap, high value): concurrent flushes.** Fire the per-type / per-label UNWIND batches with `asyncio.gather` instead of awaiting sequentially. Directly attacks the round-trips × latency term. Note FalkorDB serializes writes per graph, so this hides *network* latency rather than server work — the server-side cost is addressed by #282.

**Stage 2 (opt-in): cross-document write buffer.** Accumulate nodes/edges across documents and flush per type at full batch size (e.g. a batch-session context manager with explicit flush). Must be **opt-in**: today each document is atomic-ish with its own `IngestionResult`, and a shared buffer changes failure attribution — a silent behavior change would break per-doc error handling.

## Related failure-mode multiplier

The per-item fallback (`graph_store.py:232-249`) degrades one failing 500-row batch into 500 sequential queries. At production scale this turns a transient batch error into minutes of extra latency. Worth bounding or logging loudly as part of this work.

Related: #282 (range indexes — the server-side half of the same slowdown).

title: [Issue] perf(storage): auto-create range indexes on id — writes degrade to label scans as the graph grows
description:
# Auto-create range indexes on `id` — writes currently degrade to label scans

## Problem

`ensure_indices()` (`src/graphrag_sdk/storage/vector_store.py:588`) creates only **vector** and **fulltext** indexes. No range (exact-match) index is ever created on the `id` property, yet the entire write path keys on it:

- **Node upserts** — `MERGE (n:`Label` {id: item.id})` (`storage/graph_store.py:108`): label scan per UNWIND row.
- **Relationship upserts** — `MATCH (a:`Src` {id}), (b:`Tgt` {id})` (`storage/graph_store.py:212-227`): **two** label scans per edge row, typically against `__Entity__` or `Chunk`.
- **Mentions writes** (`_write_mentions`) — same pattern.
- **Update/delete machinery** — `delete_document` commit point, `has_pending_delete`, `delete_stale_relationships`, orphan cleanup: all `MATCH ... {id: $id}`.

Cost is quadratic over the life of the graph: each batch scans a graph made bigger by all previous batches. At a production deployment's scale (~290K nodes / 1.2M edges), one 500-row edge batch performs up to 1,000 endpoint lookups × ~137K-node label scans ≈ **~137M node visits for a single UNWIND query**. This is the dominant server-side write cost and the main reason ingestion "gets slower the more you load."

Reported from two independent production/POC deployments.

## Fix

1. Add range indexes to `ensure_indices()`:
   - `CREATE INDEX FOR (n:__Entity__) ON (n.id)`
   - `CREATE INDEX FOR (n:Chunk) ON (n.id)`
   - `CREATE INDEX FOR (n:Document) ON (n.id)`

   FalkorDB's `CREATE INDEX` errors when the index exists; the existing `_INDEX_EXISTS_MARKERS` handling (`vector_store.py:27,112`) already makes this idempotent — reuse it.

2. **Trap: `__Entity__(id)` does not accelerate node MERGEs.** Node upserts merge on the *specific* label (`Person`, `Team`, …) — `__Entity__` is added by a later `SET` (`graph_store.py:111-112`), and with open schemas the label set isn't known at setup. Create per-label indexes **lazily** in `upsert_nodes`: keep a set of ensured labels on the `GraphStore` instance; on first sight of a new label, fire the idempotent `CREATE INDEX` before the UNWIND. One extra round trip per new label per process.

## Verification

- `GRAPH.EXPLAIN` on an upsert query must show an index scan (not a label scan) for the endpoint lookups.
- Test asserting `ensure_indices()` issues the range-index DDL, and that `upsert_nodes` ensures a label's index exactly once.

## Workaround for existing deployments (works today, mid-ingestion)

```
GRAPH.QUERY <graph> "CREATE INDEX FOR (n:__Entity__) ON (n.id)"
GRAPH.QUERY <graph> "CREATE INDEX FOR (n:Chunk) ON (n.id)"
GRAPH.QUERY <graph> "CREATE INDEX FOR (n:Document) ON (n.id)"
```

Each errors harmlessly if already present. Note: FalkorDB builds indexes in the background — queries don't benefit until construction finishes (minutes on a ~300K-node graph).

title: [Issue] Ontology learning: auto-discover schema from a corpus
description:
## Problem

The SDK requires a fixed ontology (entity types, relationship types, properties) defined before ingestion. For users exploring an unknown corpus, picking the right ontology upfront is hard and usually wrong on the first pass.

## Goal

Auto-discover an ontology from input documents and propose it for user approval, rather than requiring it as a precondition. Reproduces the v0 `Ontology.from_sources(sources, model, boundaries)` capability on top of the v1 schema model.

## Foundation (already landed / in flight)

#260 / PR #256 establishes the foundation this issue builds on:

- Typed `PropertyType` on `EntityType` and `RelationType`.
- `GraphSchema.merge()` for unioning schemas across documents.
- `GraphSchema.from_file` / `save_to_file` for the schema-as-config artifact.
- Data-graph inference (`OntologyStore.infer()`) — pulls today's working ontology back out of FalkorDB.

So an auto-discovery pass has a clean target: a `GraphSchema` it can synthesize, save to disk, and re-load on the next ingest.

## Proposed API

```python
draft = await GraphSchema.from_sources(
    sources,
    llm,
    boundaries="biotech research papers about CRISPR",
    sample_chunks_per_doc=3,
)
draft.save_to_file("ontology.json")  # user edits / curates
GraphRAG(..., schema=GraphSchema.from_file("ontology.json"))
```

Behavior:

- Sample N chunks per document → batched LLM calls proposing entity types + relation types + their typed properties (with descriptions).
- Merge per-document drafts via `GraphSchema.merge()`.
- Return a `GraphSchema` the user can inspect, edit, save, and reuse.
- Optional iterative refinement: re-running `from_sources` on additional docs unions cleanly into an existing schema.

## Roadmap

Phase 5.7 — Ontology Learning.

## Acceptance

- [ ] `GraphSchema.from_sources` returns a non-trivial draft for a small test corpus.
- [ ] Drafts round-trip through `save_to_file` / `from_file` without loss.
- [ ] Documentation and one example notebook.
- [ ] (Stretch) Iterative refinement against an existing on-disk schema.

## Depends on

- #260 (foundation: typed properties, schema serialization, data-graph inference)

title: [Issue] Ontology evolution: deferred follow-ups from #268
description:
Tracks known deferrals from #268 (mutating evolution API). Not blockers; each can ship independently.

### 1. Relation-attribute evolution

`add_attribute`, `drop_attribute`, and `rename_attribute` raise `NotImplementedError` on relation owners today. The workaround is `delete_all()` + re-ingest. To lift it we need a edge-property migration primitive on `GraphStore` (iterate edges of a given type, SET / REMOVE / coerce property) plus an analogue of `_run_atomic_attribute_backfill` that scans candidate co-mention chunks instead of `MENTIONED_IN`.

### 2. Surface failing chunk content on `OntologyEvolutionError`

When `add_attribute` hard-fails on a chunk, the exception carries `failed_chunks: list[str]` (ids only). Users have no way to inspect *why* without manually requerying. Add `failed_chunks_detail: list[FailedChunk]` carrying `chunk_id`, `chunk_text`, the raw LLM response, and the parse error. Lets users decide to fix the chunk content, ignore that one chunk, or report a prompt bug.

### 3. `OntologyEvolutionError` reusable escape hatch

Once #2 lands, consider an `add_attribute(..., skip_chunks: list[str] = [])` parameter so a caller can deliberately exclude known-bad chunks on retry without breaking the alignment invariant for everything else.

### 4. Cost preview enrichments

`dry_run=True` returns `chunks_in_scope`. Enrich with an estimated token count (chunk text + prompt template lengths) so users can plug their per-token price in and get a real cost number instead of "~one LLM call per chunk."

### 5. Provenance on backfilled non-RELATES edges

`backfill_relation_pattern` deliberately skips `source_chunk_ids` because `GraphStore.upsert_relationships` only unions provenance for `:RELATES`. Teach the upsert path to union provenance for any edge type that already carries the field, then re-enable provenance writes on backfilled edges so they're traceable. Labels: enhancement

title: [PR] feat(ontology): mutating evolution API — add/drop/rename + atomic attribute backfill
description:
## Summary

Follow-on to #256. PR #256 introduced a persistent ontology graph and a strict-by-default `OntologyStore.register()` that admits new labels but refuses any modification to an existing one. This PR adds the public seam to actually *evolve* the ontology after first ingest, under a strict design invariant: **a declared attribute is queryable on every instance of its owner entity type** — the SDK exposes no API that can declare schema your data doesn't match.

## The 15-method API surface

Every method is `async`, grouped by what it touches.

### Group 1 — Pure declarations (cheap, no LLM) — returns `Ontology`
- `set_entity_description`, `set_relation_description`, `set_attribute_description`
- `add_entity` (declaration only)
- `add_relation_pattern` (declaration only)

### Group 2 — Mechanical data migration (Cypher, no LLM) — returns `Ontology`
Data migration runs first; ontology graph is updated second. Idempotent on crash.
- `rename_entity`, `rename_attribute`, `rename_relation`
- `drop_entity` (cascades to relation patterns), `drop_relation`, `drop_relation_pattern`

### Group 3 — Atomic attribute evolution (LLM, invariant-enforcing) — returns `EvolutionResult`
The commit point is the ontology graph write — last. Backfill runs first; hard failures raise `OntologyEvolutionError` without committing the schema change.
- `add_attribute(owner_label, attribute, *, concurrency=4, dry_run=False)` — declare + LLM backfill across chunks mentioning the owner + ontology commit, atomically. Entity owners only.
- `drop_attribute(owner_label, name)` — REMOVE on every instance + ontology delete. Entity owners only.

Type changes go through `drop_attribute` + `add_attribute` (the LLM re-derives values from chunks — the only honest move when text is the source of truth). There is intentionally no `retype_attribute`.

### Group 4 — Opportunistic discovery (opt-in, not invariant-enforcing) — returns `BackfillResult`
- `backfill_entity(label, *, scope, concurrency=4, dry_run=False)` — re-scan chunks for any entities of this type you might have missed.
- `backfill_relation_pattern(rel_label, source, target, *, dry_run=False)` — re-scan candidate co-mention chunks for any edges of this pattern.

Declaring an entity type or relation pattern is "this is allowed," not "this exists." Zero instances is a valid state. Use these tools to opportunistically populate from the existing corpus when you want to.

## Concurrency

**Evolution calls are not safe to run concurrently with `ingest()` or with each other on the same graph.** The extractor reads the persisted ontology, and Group 2 / Group 4 calls use count-then-mutate Cypher across two statements. Gate evolution behind an application-level lock in multi-process deployments.

## Cost preview (`dry_run=True`)

`add_attribute`, `backfill_entity`, and `backfill_relation_pattern` accept `dry_run=True`. The scope query runs (cheap); the LLM is not invoked; the result carries `chunks_in_scope` so you can preview cost

## Summary

Wires declared `Attribute` properties on `Entity` / `Relation` types from the local `Ontology` through extraction, storage, and retrieval. The ontology persists in a dedicated `<data_graph>__ontology` FalkorDB graph and accumulates **new labels** across ingest passes; existing labels are frozen by `OntologyStore.register()` to keep the ontology aligned with the data graph (extending an existing label is an ontology-evolution operation reserved for a future API).

**Forward-only over time**: nodes ingested before a property was declared remain without that property; FalkorDB's `MERGE … SET n += props` writes new keys naturally and `WHERE p.attr > N` excludes nodes that never received the key — no backfill machinery.

title: [Issue] Schema-driven attributes: typed properties through extraction → storage → retrieval
description:
## Problem

The SDK's `GraphSchema` already supports `PropertyType` declarations (`STRING` / `INTEGER` / `FLOAT` / `BOOLEAN` / `DATE` / `LIST`), but they're dead code: never read during extraction, never written to the graph, never surfaced in retrieval prompts. Structured attributes like `Person.age:INTEGER` or `Person.birth_date:DATE` can't be filtered, sorted, or aggregated over by the LLM.

## Goal

Make declared properties land in the graph and be usable in retrieval queries:

- Extract typed attribute values during ingestion.
- Store them on graph nodes / relationships.
- Surface them in the Cypher generation prompt so the LLM can author `WHERE p.age > 30`, `ORDER BY p.founded_year DESC`, etc.

## Status

Tracked in PR #256.

### Scope (delivered)

- `RelationType.properties` (entities had it; relations did not).
- Typed-attribute extraction in the LLM verify-and-extract prompt; coerced to declared types at the extractor boundary; `required=True` failures drop the record.
- Schema validation in the ingestion pipeline (drops undeclared keys, drops nodes missing required attrs, cascades dangling-rel cleanup).
- Cypher generation prompt auto-built from the live ontology (no more hardcoded property list); synthesized numeric-attribute examples per declared `INTEGER`/`FLOAT` property.
- Ontology inferred from the data graph at retrieval time (`db.labels()` + `keys()`/`typeof()` sampling), merged with the user-supplied local schema so declared descriptions and `required` flags survive.
- `GraphSchema.save_to_file` / `from_file` for schema-as-config; `GraphRAG.save_ontology(path)` helper.

### Explicitly out of scope (separate issues)

- Auto-discover ontology from a corpus → #240
- TTL / OWL import → follow-up
- `unique` flag on properties (v0 had this — drove MERGE-key dedup) → follow-up

## Acceptance

- [ ] PR #256 merged.
- [ ] Schemas without declared properties produce identical output to the prior pipeline (regression-clean).
- [ ] End-to-end smoke: declare `Person.age:INTEGER`, ingest a doc that mentions ages, ask "who is older than 50?" through `kg.chat_session()`, get back a filtered list.

title: [PR] feat(retrieval): CypherFirstAggregationStrategy + cypher-path accuracy fixes
description:
## Summary

Adds a new opt-in retrieval strategy, `CypherFirstAggregationStrategy`, that routes quantitative/structural questions ("how many", "which X has the most", "BOTH A and B", "are there any X without Y", "what is the average …") through a deterministic Cypher-first path. Non-aggregation questions delegate to `MultiPathRetrieval` unchanged.

Alongside the strategy, this PR also lands six targeted SDK-level fixes to the pre-existing cypher path (used by `MultiPathRetrieval(enable_cypher=True)` too): smart `LIMIT` injection, `APOC`/`GDS`/`db.*` function-call blocklist in the validator, 0-row label-widen fallback, two new schema-prompt examples, and metadata threading for observability.

## Background

A focused failure-mode investigation on a 56-person / 10-org synthetic benchmark identified seven distinct failure modes on aggregation questions — none of them random one-offs:

- Cypher results encoded as `\" | \"`-joined strings lose column names, so the answer-LLM can swap row values
- Auto `LIMIT 25` truncates group-by aggregations silently
- `apoc.text.regexGroups(...)`-style function calls slipped past the `CALL` blocklist
- Typed-label cypher queries fail when extraction labeled the entity differently
- Schema prompt had no examples for "BOTH X AND Y" or top-N group-by
- Empty cypher results were treated identically for positive and negation existentials
- Roles/projects extracted as free text in chunks weren't queryable as typed nodes

The new strategy directly addresses each one. The 7-question failure-mode benchmark went from **2-5/7** (depending on which pre-fix variant) to **7/7 stable** across three runs.

## What's in this PR (4 commits)

| Commit | Title |
|---|---|
| \`bb920c6\` | improve text-to-Cypher accuracy on aggregation questions |
| \`7fa7a1f\` | add CypherFirstAggregationStrategy |
| \`deaa64d\` | pre-merge review fixes for CypherFirstAggregationStrategy |
| \`d818eb1\` | split CypherFirst into path classes + pluggable extractor |

Each commit has its own detailed body.

## Compatibility (cypher-off callers)

The PR is **additive** for users who don't opt in:
- `CypherFirstAggregationStrategy` only runs if passed explicitly as `retrieval_strategy=`
- The cypher-path improvements (smart LIMIT, APOC blocklist, etc.) live inside the cypher generation/execution code and only run when `enable_cypher=True`
- The "Authoritative Graph Query Results" system-prompt rule is added conditionally — only when the retriever produced a cypher_results section. With cypher off, the base system prompt is **byte-identical** to main.

Test coverage (\`tests/test_facade.py::TestCypherAuthorityRuleInjection\`) pins the contract.

## Usage

    CypherFirstAggregationStrategy,
    FastCorefResolver,
    GraphExtraction,
    LLMVerifiedResolution,
    SentenceTokenCapChunking,
)

extractor = GraphExtraction(llm=llm, coref_resolver=Fast

title: [PR] fix(retrieval): rank MENTIONED_IN chunks by cosine in MultiPath Path C
description:
## Summary

`retrieve_chunks` Path C uses `COLLECT(c)[..3]` with no `ORDER BY`. For hub entities — the main product name, generic verbs like "install", high-frequency Cypher keywords — this picks **an arbitrary 3 out of hundreds**, almost never the chunks relevant to the current query.

This PR adds an `ORDER BY vec.cosineDistance(c.embedding, query_vector)` before the `COLLECT` so per-entity chunk selection is query-aware. Closes the retrieval half of #258.

## Repro / Evidence

Tested against the FalkorDB docs knowledge graph (1,356 chunks, 2,945 entities). The `FalkorDB` entity has **486 chunks** linked via `MENTIONED_IN`. Six of those are install-relevant (chunks 0, 1, 2, 3, 6, 7 of `getting-started/index.md`).

P(an unordered 3 of 486 contains an install chunk) ≈ 4% per slot → ~12% chance overall. Measured behavior matches: standalone `How do I install FalkorDB?` reliably failed.

**Before** (arbitrary 3):
> "This isn't covered in the FalkorDB docs. Related setup topics include Docker, Kubernetes, and the Python client installation."

**After** (cosine-ranked 3):
> "FalkorDB can be deployed with Docker, including the `falkordb/falkordb-server` image, and there's also a Helm chart installation path for Kubernetes. For Python, `pip install falkordb` installs the FalkorDB client."

Same query, same graph, same retrieval strategy — only `chunk_retrieval.py:Path C` changed.

## The change

```diff
- MATCH (e:__Entity__ {id: eid})-[:MENTIONED_IN]->(c:Chunk)
- WITH eid, COLLECT(c)[..3] AS chunks
+ MATCH (e:__Entity__ {id: eid})-[:MENTIONED_IN]->(c:Chunk)
+ WHERE c.embedding IS NOT NULL
+ WITH eid, c, vec.cosineDistance(c.embedding, vecf32($qv)) AS dist
+ ORDER BY eid, dist ASC
+ WITH eid, COLLECT(c)[..3] AS chunks
```

`query_vector` is already passed into `retrieve_chunks` — used by Path B (raw vector search) — so it's a parameter-add, not a new signature. Chunks without stored embeddings are excluded (rare; `c.embedding IS NOT NULL` guard).

## Tests

Added `test_mentioned_in_ranks_chunks_by_cosine` to `tests/test_multi_path_retrieval.py`, asserting the emitted Cypher contains `vec.cosineDistance`, `ORDER BY`, and passes the query vector as a parameter. Full retrieval test suite passes (161/161, 1 skip).

## Test plan

- [x] Unit tests pass (`pytest tests/test_multi_path_retrieval.py` — 45/45)
- [x] Broader retrieval suite passes (`pytest -k 'retrieval or multi_path or chunk'` — 161/161 + 1 skip)
- [x] Live end-to-end repro on FalkorDB docs widget: failing query now answers correctly with cited install commands
- [ ] Reviewer to sanity-check perf on graphs with very large MENTIONED_IN fan-out (per-entity ordering is O(N log N) per entity, but N is bounded per entity by ingestion characteristics)

title: [Issue] Loader: strip static-site-generator templating (Jekyll/Hugo/etc.) before embedding chunks
description:
## Problem

When ingesting markdown files served by static-site generators (Jekyll, Hugo, MkDocs, Docusaurus), the source `.md` contains template directives — Liquid tags `{% ... %}`, expressions `{{ ... }}`, YAML front matter — that the renderer strips before serving HTML. The SDK ingests them as-is, so they enter the chunker and get embedded alongside actual content.

These directives are semantically noise but dominate the surface form of short chunks. Retrieval recall on heavily-templated pages is significantly worse than it should be.

## Evidence

GraphRAG-SDK powers the FalkorDB docs widget (docs.falkordb.com). The docs site is built with Jekyll. `getting-started/index.md` wraps every install command in `{% capture pypi_0 %} pip install falkordb {% endcapture %}` … `{% include code_tabs.html %}` blocks.

Raw vector search (`db.idx.vector.queryNodes`, top-50) for `"how to install falkordb?"`:

| | install-doc chunk rank | cosine |
|---|---|---|
| Before preprocessing | **#35** | 0.397 |
| After stripping Jekyll | **#4** | 0.433 |

End-to-end widget answers also flipped from `"This isn't covered in the FalkorDB docs"` → actual install instructions for `"I need to install anything?"` and `"how to install falkordb?"`.

## What we did locally

~10-line cleaner applied before `rag.ingest(...)`:

```python
def strip_jekyll(text: str) -> str:
    if text.startswith("---\n"):
        end = text.find("\n---\n", 4)
        if end != -1:
            text = text[end + 5:]
    text = re.sub(r"\{%-?.*?-?%\}", "", text, flags=re.DOTALL)
    text = re.sub(r"\{\{.*?\}\}",   "", text, flags=re.DOTALL)
    text = re.sub(r"[ \t]+\n", "\n", text)
    text = re.sub(r"\n{3,}", "\n\n", text)
    return text.strip()
```

Content inside Liquid tag *pairs* (e.g. the command between `{% capture %}` / `{% endcapture %}`) is kept — only the directives are removed.

## Suggested fix

Either:
1. **Preprocessor hook on ingestion** — `rag.ingest(..., preprocess=fn)` so consumers can clean content before chunking without subclassing strategies.
2. **Built-in `MarkdownLoader`** with `strip_templating=True` (Jekyll/Liquid first; extend later to Hugo `{{< >}}`, MDX, Docusaurus admonitions).

Option 2 fits the loader-coverage theme of #241 and is more discoverable.

title: [PR] docs(retrieval): recommend SentenceTokenCapChunking for CypherFirst
description:
## Summary

Adds a "Recommended ingestion config" section to `CypherFirstAggregationStrategy`'s docstring pointing users at `SentenceTokenCapChunking`. Cosmetic / discoverability — the strategy itself works the same.

## Why

The default chunker (`FixedSizeChunking`) splits on a character window with no awareness of sentence or word boundaries, so entity names get truncated at chunk boundaries (`"Wayne Enterprises"` → `"Wayne En"`). The stub entities never merge with their full forms during resolution, so cypher counts come back inflated.

On the internal 7-question aggregation benchmark, switching the benchmark's ingestion config from `FixedSizeChunking(chunk_size=1000)` to `SentenceTokenCapChunking(max_tokens=512, overlap_sentences=2)` moved the score from **6/7** (intermittent) to **7/7** (stable across three runs).

## Stacking

title: [PR] feat(ingestion): default to SentenceTokenCapChunking in ingest()/upda…
description:
…te()

Changes the default chunker that ``GraphRAG.ingest()`` and ``GraphRAG.update()`` fall back to when the caller doesn't pass an explicit ``chunker=``. Was ``FixedSizeChunking()``; now ``SentenceTokenCapChunking()`` (sentence-aware, max_tokens=512, overlap_sentences=2 — the strategy's own defaults).

Why
---
``FixedSizeChunking`` splits on a hard character window with no awareness of sentence, word, or paragraph boundaries. When the window cuts through an entity name, the per-chunk LLM extractor produces a stub entity for the fragment (``"Wayne Enterprises"`` → ``"Wayne En"`` in chunk N plus unparsable text in chunk N+1). These stubs never merge with their full forms during resolution because their embeddings differ enough that LLMVerifiedResolution scores them below the soft threshold.

This silently inflates cypher counts and pollutes "which X" lists. The strategy that surfaced this — ``CypherFirstAggregationStrategy`` — was hitting a 6/7 ceiling on the internal aggregation benchmark with one question failing because of these stubs. Switching to ``SentenceTokenCapChunking`` cleared the benchmark to 7/7 stable across three runs, and the post-ingest graph state went from 11-14 organization nodes (including ``Glo`` / ``Initech System`` / ``Wayne En``) to exactly 10 clean orgs, and from 66-80 ``Person`` nodes (with ``Carla`` / ``Carla Okafor`` duplicates) to exactly 56 distinct persons — matching the corpus.

A side benefit: sentence-aware chunks with 2-sentence overlap almost always keep a person's first mention in the same chunk as their later short-form references, so per-chunk FastCoref now binds ``Carla → Carla Okafor`` reliably. That eliminates the short-form-duplicate class too, not just the truncation stubs.

Compatibility
-------------
``FixedSizeChunking`` remains exported and fully supported — callers who explicitly pass ``chunker=FixedSizeChunking()`` get unchanged behavior. Existing tests (748 passed, 24 skipped) pass without modification: no test in the suite asserts on chunk count or content shape from the default chunker, so switching defaults doesn't break the suite.

Callers who relied on the previous default and want to keep it should pass ``chunker=FixedSizeChunking()`` explicitly. The docstrings call out the new default and reference ``FixedSizeChunking`` as the opt-in character-window alternative.

title: [Issue] feat(retrieval): accept history + rewrite_question_with_history in retrieve()
description:
## Context
`GraphRAG.completion(question, history=, rewrite_question_with_history=True)` is a great affordance for the common "user asks a vague follow-up that references earlier turns" case. But callers who build their own retrieval+prompt pipeline (rather than using `completion()` directly) currently can't get history-aware retrieval out of the box:

```python
# Current SDK retrieve() signature — no history support
retrieve(self, question: str, *, strategy=None, reranker=None, ctx=None) -> RetrieverResult
```

If a downstream caller wants history-aware retrieval, they have to re-implement the rewrite step themselves (one extra LLM call), or refactor to use `completion()` and give up custom prompt/citation handling.

## Concrete downstream case
FalkorDB/GraphRAG-UI's `RagService.query` does its own numbered-citation prompt building. Q2 in a widget conversation:

- Q1: "how to start work with the graphragsdk?" → good answer
- Q2: "give me the python that needed to do that" → **"If you mean the GraphRAG SDK, it isn't documented here. Please use the Contact Support button."**

The literal text of Q2 contains "python" but not "GraphRAG SDK". Retrieval matched FalkorDB Python Client chunks instead of GraphRAG-SDK chunks; the LLM had history (so it understood the user meant the SDK) but the retrieval didn't. The LLM reconciled the mismatch by hallucinating a refusal — a real prod-visible quality issue.

We're implementing a local rewrite step in our `RagService` (one extra LLM call before retrieval), but it duplicates logic that already exists in the SDK's `completion()`.

## Proposed API
Add `history` and `rewrite_question_with_history` kwargs to `retrieve()`, mirroring `completion()`'s shape:

```python
async def retrieve(
    self,
    question: str,
    *,
    history: list[ChatMessage | dict[str, str]] | None = None,
    rewrite_question_with_history: bool = False,
    strategy: RetrievalStrategy | None = None,
    reranker: RerankingStrategy | None = None,
    ctx: Context | None = None,
) -> RetrieverResult
```

Semantics: if `rewrite_question_with_history=True` and `history` is non-empty, the SDK internally calls the rewrite (same logic as `completion()`) and runs `retrieval.search(rewritten_question, ctx)`. The returned `RetrieverResult` is unchanged in shape; optionally surface the rewritten question on `RetrieverResult.metadata` for debuggability.

## Alternative
Expose `rewrite_question(question, history) -> str` as a standalone utility. Lower-level but useful for callers who want to log/cache the rewrite separately.

## Acceptance
- `retrieve(history=..., rewrite_question_with_history=True)` works end-to-end
- Reuses the same rewrite prompt + LLM call path as `completion()` (single source of truth)
- Backwards compatible — both new kwargs default to None / False

title: [PR] feat(api): forward loader/chunker/extractor/resolver from apply_changes to ingest/update
description:
## Summary
`apply_changes` is the documented single entrypoint for CI-driven incremental ingestion (`graph.apply_changes(**parse_git_diff(...))` in the v1.1.0 release notes), but the public signature accepts only `added` / `modified` / `deleted` plus concurrency knobs — there is no way to pass per-call strategy overrides. Internally it dispatches to `ingest()` and `update()` with SDK defaults, so any caller who wanted a custom chunker/extractor/resolver had to bypass `apply_changes` entirely and loop over the primitives themselves.

This PR adds `loader=`, `chunker=`, `extractor=`, `resolver=` kwargs to `apply_changes` (and the sync wrapper) and forwards them to the inner `ingest()` and `update()` dispatches. `delete_document` does not take strategies and is unaffected. Defaults are all `None` — fully backwards compatible.

## Motivation
The downstream GraphRAG-UI docs-CI orchestrator builds a per-graph `IngestionConfig` (GLiNER threshold 0.75, `SentenceTokenCapChunking(256, 2)`, `LLMVerifiedResolution`) and then calls `apply_changes`. Without this forwarding, our strategies are silently dropped at the SDK boundary — the orchestrator either has to call the primitives directly (losing `apply_changes`'s batch-level concurrency control and uniform `BatchEntry` error surface) or accept SDK-default ingestion (silent retrieval quality drift).

## Changes
- `apply_changes(*, ..., loader=None, chunker=None, extractor=None, resolver=None, ...)` — four new kwargs

title: [PR] feat(v1.1.0): incremental ingestion primitives with crash-safe cutover
description:
Adds three new public methods on GraphRAG so consumers can re-sync the knowledge graph after their source documents change, without rebuilding from scratch:

  - update(source, document_id=..., if_missing=...)
  - delete_document(document_id)
  - apply_changes(added=..., modified=..., deleted=...)

The cutover is a documented state machine
(EMPTY -> WRITING -> WRITTEN -> COMMITTED -> FINAL) keyed off a ready_to_commit marker on the pending Document node. The single Cypher SET that flips that marker is the commit point: it must complete before any destructive op touches the live document. Once committed, every subsequent op is idempotent and crash-recovery rolls forward rather than back. update() interrupted by a transient failure now retries cleanly instead of raising DocumentNotFoundError against a half-deleted document.

apply_changes splits its concurrency knob: max_concurrency=3 (adds, unchanged) and update_concurrency=1 (modifies, forced by the orphan- cleanup invariant — pipeline.run() must persist MENTIONED_IN edges before returning so concurrent updates sharing an entity always observe at least one incident edge). The docstring names the invariant; an integration test (test_concurrent_updates_preserve_ shared_entity) is the tripwire that protects the default.

Folds in a pre-existing silent-correctness bug: pipeline._write_mentions consumed pre-resolution entity ids, so MENTIONED_IN edges silently failed to write for any entity merged by SemanticResolution or LLMVerifiedResolution. v1.1.0's orphan cleanup would have inherited that breakage. Resolvers now expose a remap dict on ResolutionResult; pipeline rewrites graph_data.mentions through it between resolve and write. Default ExactMatch users see no behavior change.

Test coverage:
  - 33 new unit tests (state machine, mention remap, docstring tripwire)
  - 8 parametrized integration tests (4 invariant cases x 2 resolvers) in test_integration.py::TestIncrementalUpdateInvariants
  - New CI integration job runs them against a real FalkorDB service container; existing CI continues to skip via RUN_INTEGRATION gate

Public surface additions: UpdateResult, DeleteDocumentResult, ApplyChangesResult, DocumentNotFoundError, Document.content_hash and Document.ready_to_commit properties. document_id now accepted in file-mode ingest() (defaults to os.path.normpath(source)). No breaking changes.

title: [Issue] Expose token usage stats on ingest/completion/retrieve responses
description:
## Problem

The SDK responses (`ingest()`, `completion()`, `retrieve()`) don't expose LLM/embedding token usage. Users who want cost tracking must subclass internal private methods (`_raw_embed_async`, `_completion_kwargs`, `_messages_completion_kwargs`) — a fragile pattern that breaks on internal refactors.

Both `benchmark.py` and the benchmark harness in the demo repo use this pattern, demonstrating the demand.

## Expected behavior

Response objects should include usage information:

```python
result = await rag.ingest(source_id, text=text)
print(result.usage.prompt_tokens)       # total LLM input tokens
print(result.usage.completion_tokens)   # total LLM output tokens
print(result.usage.embedding_tokens)    # total embedding tokens

result = await rag.completion(question)
print(result.usage.prompt_tokens)
print(result.usage.completion_tokens)
print(result.usage.embedding_tokens)
```

## Context

- Every user doing cost analysis, billing dashboards, or LLM observability needs this
- The demo repo has two independent implementations of tracking wrappers — both relying on private internals
- LiteLLM already returns usage on every response; the SDK just doesn't surface it

## Priority

High — required for production cost monitoring.

title: [PR] feat: introduce StructuralChunking, add MarkdownLoader
description:
#241 Feature: Document-Aware Structural Chunking & Refactored Ingestion Pipeline

Hi guys, I would like to share some ideas about document loaders and structural chunking. 

## Summary

This Pull Request introduces a structural-aware document ingestion pipeline designed to significantly improve retrieval precision in RAG scenarios. It transitions the chunking architecture from being purely text-based to operating on complex document structures (such as tables, lists, and hierarchical headers) are never broken arbitrarily.

## Changes

- **ChunkingStrategy Interface**: Added a new method chunk_document(document: DocumentOutput, ctx: Context).
- **Pipeline Update**: The ingestion pipeline now passes the full DocumentOutput object to the chunker rather than just the raw text.
- **Backward Compatibility**: By default, chunk_document delegates to the legacy chunk(document.text) method. Format-agnostic text chunkers continue to work exactly as before, while advanced strategies can tap into document.elements.

## Test Plan

- [x] All existing tests pass (`pytest tests/ -q`)
- [x] New tests added for new functionality (if applicable)
- [x] Lint passes (`ruff check src/`)

## Notes

1. Generic Document Model (DocumentElement)
Introduced a new hierarchical data model in core/models.py. Loaders now parse documents into a list of DocumentElements. Each node retains its original content, structural type (paragraph, table, code, etc.), and spatial breadcrumbs (e.g., ["Chapter 1", "Section 1.2"]).

2. Robust Markdown Parsing (markdown-it-py)
Replaced the brittle Regex/State-Machine parsing in MarkdownLoader with markdown-it-py (fully CommonMark compliant).

The loader now deterministically loops through Semantic Tokens (table_open, bullet_list_open, etc.) to perfectly map markdown lines to DocumentElements, completely eliminating the risk of malformed tables or nested lists.

3. StructuralChunking Strategy
Introduced a powerful, format-agnostic chunker that groups DocumentElements dynamically up to a max_tokens cap:

- Smart Fallback: If a single element (e.g., a massive 400-line table) exceeds the token cap, it delegates the splitting to a fallback_chunker (like SentenceTokenCapChunking).

- Fragment Indexing (Anti-Amnesia): When oversized elements are sliced, the chunker actively prepends the contextual breadcrumb and a sequential index to each sub-chunk (e.g., Header 1 > Header 2 [Part 1/3]). This ensures the LLM and the Vector Store retain perfect spatial awareness during Retrieval.

4. ContextualChunking as a Decorator
Refactored ContextualChunking to act as a wrapper/decorator over a base_chunker. It receives the pre-chunked list and focuses entirely on executing high-performance batch LLM calls to enrich the chunks with global context.

title: [PR] fix(retrieval): preserve full Document.path in chunk citations
description:
## Summary
- \`fetch_chunk_documents\` was truncating \`Document.path\` to a basename before returning, throwing away the directory part of the path.

A consumer (the GraphRAG-UI chat widget) is using \`source_doc\` to render clickable links to the deployed docs site. title: [PR] Security/review fixes
description:
This pull request releases version 1.0.1 of the `graphrag-sdk`, focusing on security, API correctness, and improved type safety. It introduces breaking changes to the public API, tightens dependency version constraints, and improves documentation and examples for safer and more consistent usage. Key changes include eliminating Cypher injection risks, adding TLS support, refining ingestion and finalization APIs, and updating all relevant documentation and examples to match the new contracts.

**Security and API Hardening:**

* Eliminated Cypher injection surfaces in `VectorStore` by replacing parameterized index methods with named variants and ensuring all Cypher queries use literal identifiers. The `embedding_dimension` is now bound-checked, and the `similarity_function` parameter is dropped. Search methods are split into per-target variants for safety.
* Added TLS support to `ConnectionConfig` with new SSL-related fields, and updated `from_url` to auto-enable TLS for `rediss://` URLs, raising on unknown schemes. title: [Issue] Emit typed relationship edges at extraction time instead of RELATES
description:
## Problem

Currently the pipeline writes relationships as:

```
(:__Entity__)-[:RELATES {rel_type: "USES", fact: "...", ...}]->(:__Entity__)
```

Then either `finalize()` (proposed in #225) or user postprocessing promotes them to:

```
(:__Entity__)-[:USES {fact: "...", ...}]->(:__Entity__)
```

This is a double write — the extractor already knows the relationship type at extraction time.

## Proposed optimization

In the Write pipeline step, if `rel_type` is available and non-empty, write the typed edge directly:

```cypher
MERGE (a)-[r:USES]->(b)
SET r.fact = $fact, r.description = $desc, ...
```

Fall back to `[:RELATES]` only when `rel_type` is NULL or empty.

## Benefits

- Eliminates the `finalize()` rewrite pass (fewer graph mutations)
- Graph is immediately browsable after ingest without waiting for finalize
- Simpler code path

## Considerations

- Relationship type must be sanitized to `[A-Z0-9_]+` for valid Cypher
- Deduplication in `finalize()` must handle typed edges (currently only deduplicates `RELATES`)
- This is an optimization of #225, not a replacement — `finalize()` should still clean up any remaining `RELATES` edges

## Priority

Lower — optimization that can follow #225.

title: [Issue] Stabilize LLM/Embedder extension points (or document subclass pattern)
description:
## Problem

Users who need custom LLM behavior (tracking, caching, rate limiting) must subclass and override private methods:

- `LiteLLM._completion_kwargs()`
- `LiteLLM._messages_completion_kwargs()`
- `LiteLLMEmbedder._raw_embed_async()`

These are undocumented internal methods. If renamed or refactored, all custom subclasses break silently.

## Proposed solution

Either:

**A) Stabilize these as public API** — rename to `completion_kwargs()` / `embed_async()`, document them, add to the public interface contract.

**B) Provide an official `InstrumentedLLM` mixin** that handles the common patterns:

```python
from graphrag_sdk import LiteLLM, InstrumentedMixin

class MyLLM(InstrumentedMixin, LiteLLM):
    def on_completion(self, response):
        # called after every LLM call with the full response
        log_tokens(response.usage)
```

**C) Deprecate subclassing in favor of hooks** (see #230) — but document the interim pattern for users who need it now.

## Context

- The demo repo has two independent `TrackingLLM` classes using these private methods
- The `EntityExtractor` ABC is a good example of a stable extension point — LLM/Embedder should follow the same pattern
- This is blocking for any production observability integration

## Priority

Lower — can be resolved by #230 (hooks), but should be documented in the interim.

title: [Issue] Add ingest progress callback / async event stream
description:
## Problem

During `rag.ingest()`, the SDK provides no progress feedback. For larger documents or multi-file ingestion, the user sees nothing between "Ingesting..." and the final result. This is problematic for:

- Long-running ingests (minutes to hours)
- UI integrations that need progress bars
- Debugging pipeline failures mid-stream

## Proposed API

```python
# Option A: callback
async def on_progress(event):
    print(f"[{event.step}] {event.message}")  # e.g. [chunking] 15/15 chunks

result = await rag.ingest(source_id, text=text, on_progress=on_progress)

# Option B: async iterator
async for event in rag.ingest_stream(source_id, text=text):
    print(f"[{event.step}] {event.message}")
```

Pipeline steps to report on:
1. Chunking (N chunks created)
2. Lexical analysis
3. Entity extraction (N entities found)
4. Quality filtering
5. Pruning
6. Resolution
7. Graph write (N nodes, N edges written)

## Context

- The 9-step pipeline (Load → Chunk → Lexical → Extract → Quality Filter → Prune → Resolve → Write → Index) can take 10-30s per document
- The demo repo just prints before/after with no visibility into what's happening
- Especially important for production ingestion of large corpora

## Priority

Lower — nice-to-have for v1.0, important for production deployments.

title: [Issue] Allow disabling rewrite/rerank stages per query
description:
## Problem

The SDK's 3-stage query pipeline (rewrite → rerank → generate) delivers high-quality answers for complex multi-hop questions, but costs 3x in LLM calls and adds ~1s latency. For simple factual queries, this overhead is unnecessary.

Users have no way to opt out of individual stages per-query.

## Proposed API

```python
# Full pipeline (default) — best for complex questions
result = await rag.completion(question)

# Skip rewrite for simple lookups
result = await rag.completion(question, rewrite=False)

# Skip rerank for latency-sensitive paths
result = await rag.completion(question, rerank=False)

# Minimal: retrieve + generate only (1 LLM call, like Neo4j's default)
result = await rag.completion(question, rewrite=False, rerank=False)
```

## Context

- The demo benchmark shows 3 LLM calls per question vs Neo4j's 1
- Average latency is 2.8s — much of it from the extra LLM round-trips
- Multi-hop and numeric questions benefit from the full pipeline; simple factual questions don't
- This would let users tune cost/quality tradeoff per-query

## Priority

Medium — important for production latency and cost optimization.

title: [Issue] Add on_llm_call / on_embed callback hooks for observability
description:
## Problem

Users who want to observe LLM/embedding calls (for logging, cost tracking, rate-limit awareness, or OpenTelemetry integration) must subclass private methods on `LiteLLM` and `LiteLLMEmbedder`. This is fragile and undocumented.

The demo repo has two independent `TrackingLLM` / `TrackingEmbedder` subclasses that override `_raw_embed_async`, `_completion_kwargs`, and `_messages_completion_kwargs`.

## Proposed API

```python
def my_llm_hook(event):
    print(f"LLM call: {event.prompt_tokens} in, {event.completion_tokens} out")

def my_embed_hook(event):
    print(f"Embed: {event.total_tokens} tokens, {len(event.texts)} texts")

rag = GraphRAG(
    ...,
    llm=LiteLLM(model="openai/gpt-4o-mini", on_call=my_llm_hook),
    embedder=LiteLLMEmbedder(model="openai/text-embedding-3-small", on_call=my_embed_hook),
)
```

Or a centralized approach:

```python
rag = GraphRAG(..., callbacks=[MyObserver()])
```

## Context

- Every production user needs this for cost dashboards and debugging
- Complements #227 (usage stats on responses) — hooks give real-time observability, response stats give per-call totals
- Avoids users depending on private method signatures

## Priority

Medium — bridges the gap until response-level usage (#227) is implemented.

title: [Issue] Add operational introspection methods to graph_store
description:
## Problem

For basic operational tasks (memory usage, slow queries, graph listing), users must drop down to `from falkordb import FalkorDB` and use raw Redis commands:

```python
db = FalkorDB(host="localhost", port=6379)
db.execute_command("GRAPH.MEMORY", "USAGE", graph_name)
db.select_graph(graph_name).slowlog()
```

This breaks the SDK abstraction and requires users to know FalkorDB internals.

## Proposed API

```python
async with GraphRAG(...) as rag:
    # Operational introspection
    mem = await rag.graph_store.memory_usage()      # GRAPH.MEMORY USAGE
    slow = await rag.graph_store.slowlog(limit=10)  # GRAPH.SLOWLOG
    info = await rag.graph_store.info()             # GRAPH.INFO
    stats = await rag.graph_store.get_statistics()  # already exists ✓
```

## Context

- `query_demo.py` in the demo repo needs 30 lines of raw FalkorDB code for ops introspection
- These are common needs for production monitoring and debugging
- `graph_store` already has a connection — it just needs thin wrappers

## Priority

Medium — important for production users, not blocking for getting-started.

title: [Issue] Allow GraphRAG constructor to accept connection params directly
description:
## Problem

Currently, users must always create a `ConnectionConfig` object:

```python
GraphRAG(
    connection=ConnectionConfig(host="localhost", graph_name="my_graph"),
    llm=..., embedder=...
)
```

This adds ceremony without flexibility. The separate config object isn't adding value for the common case.

## Proposed API

Allow flattened kwargs alongside the existing `ConnectionConfig` path:

```python
# New — simpler for getting started
GraphRAG(host="localhost", graph_name="my_graph", llm=..., embedder=...)

# Existing — still works
GraphRAG(connection=ConnectionConfig(...), llm=..., embedder=...)
```

## Context

- Every demo script repeats the `ConnectionConfig(host=..., graph_name=...)` boilerplate
- Reducing the constructor to one line lowers the perceived complexity for new users
- This is a non-breaking addition (keep `connection=` as the explicit option)

## Priority

Medium — developer experience polish.

title: [Issue] finalize(): assign human-readable names to Chunk nodes
description:
## Problem

After ingestion, Chunk nodes have no `name` property (or only a UUID), making them unreadable in FalkorDB Browser and graph exploration tools. Users must run custom Cypher to assign meaningful names.

Discovered in [graphrag-sdk-demo](https://github.com/FalkorDB/graphrag-sdk-demo) `postprocess.py`.

## Expected behavior

`rag.finalize()` should set `Chunk.name = "<source_id> · chunk <index>"` for all chunks that lack a human-readable name.

## Proposed API

```python
await rag.finalize()  # names chunks by default
# or opt-out:
await rag.finalize(name_chunks=False)
```

## Context

- The `source_id` and `chunk.index` are already available at write time
- This is a cosmetic but high-impact improvement for graph exploration UX
- The operation is idempotent (skip if name already matches)

## Priority

High — immediate quality-of-life for anyone exploring the graph visually.

title: [Issue] finalize(): promote RELATES edges to typed relationship edges
description:
## Problem

After `rag.ingest()`, the SDK writes relationships as generic `[:RELATES {rel_type: "USES"}]` edges. Users must write ~70 lines of post-processing Cypher to promote these into typed edges like `[:USES]`, `[:SUPPORTS]`, `[:INTEGRATES_WITH]`.

This was discovered in the [graphrag-sdk-demo](https://github.com/FalkorDB/graphrag-sdk-demo) where `postprocess.py` performs this rewrite manually after every ingest.

## Expected behavior

`rag.finalize()` should automatically promote `RELATES` edges into their typed equivalents using the `rel_type` property that is already extracted. All original properties (`fact`, `description`, `source_chunk_ids`, `spans`) should be preserved on the new typed edge.

## Proposed API

```python
await rag.finalize()  # promotes by default
# or opt-out:
await rag.finalize(promote_relationships=False)
```

## Context

- The extractor already produces the `rel_type` value — this is just a graph-write concern
- In the demo, 336 RELATES edges were promoted into 161 distinct typed edges
- Typed edges make the graph browsable in FalkorDB Browser and enable more expressive Cypher queries

## Priority

High — this is the #1 friction point for new users evaluating the SDK.

title: [PR] Implement tool-level error sanitization to prevent sensitive data leakage
description:
Tool handlers threw raw exceptions, so MCP clients received internal details: credentials in connection strings, IP addresses and ports, file paths, and stack traces.

## Changes

**`ErrorHandler.toMcpErrorResult()`** (`src/errors/ErrorHandler.ts`) turns any thrown value into `{ content: [{ type: "text", text: "Error: …" }], isError: true }` with a sanitized message:
- removes stack-trace frames
- `<scheme>://user:pass@host` (any scheme) → `<scheme>://<credentials>@<host>`
- database URLs without credentials (`redis`, `rediss`, `falkordb`, `falkordbs`, `mongodb`, `mongodb+srv`, `postgres`, `postgresql`) → `<scheme>://<host>`
- the address in Node network errors (`ECONNREFUSED ::1:6379`, `ENOTFOUND db.internal`), IPv4 addresses with or without a port, and `localhost:<port>`
- `password` / `token` / `apiKey` values, including quoted JSON-style ones
- absolute POSIX, `~/`, Windows and `file://` paths. A path must start a token and have at least two segments, so Cypher errors such as `expected Integer/Float` are left alone.

`AppError` messages are sanitized too. The service layer embeds raw driver messages in them (`Failed to connect to FalkorDB after 5 attempts: connect ECONNREFUSED 10.0.4.17:6379`), so passing them through would have bypassed the scrubbing. A thrown value that is not an `Error` becomes `An unexpected error occurred`.

The URL patterns bound the scheme (≤ 32 characters) and the userinfo (≤ 256 characters). Error messages can echo user query text, and the unbounded patterns backtracked quadratically: up to 32 s on a crafted 200 KB message.

**`src/mcp/tools.ts`**: all seven tools (`query_graph`, `query_graph_readonly`, `list_graphs`, `delete_graph`, `get_graph_schema`, `get_node_schema`, `get_relationship_schema`) now `return errorHandler.toMcpErrorResult(error)` instead of rethrowing. The original error is still passed to `logger.error`. Zod argument validation runs before the `try`, so invalid arguments still throw and the SDK reports them.

## Tests
- `ErrorHandler.test.ts` covers each rule, `AppError`-wrapped driver messages, harmless messages that must stay unchanged, idempotence, the long-userinfo fallback, and linear time on adversarial input.
- `tools.test.ts`: main's rejection assertions now check the `isError` result. For each of the seven tools, new tests check the sanitized result, that the original error is still logged, and how non-`Error` rejections are handled.
- Coverage of `ErrorHandler.ts` and `tools.ts` is 100% for lines and branches.

## Example

Before:
```
Error: Failed to connect to FalkorDB after 5 attempts: connect ECONNREFUSED 10.0.4.17:6379
    at /home/app/src/db.ts:45
```

After:
```
Error: Failed to connect to FalkorDB after 5 attempts: connect ECONNREFUSED <host>
```

Fixes #34

title: [PR] feat: add FALKORDB_TLS to connect over TLS
description:
Closes #80

## Summary

FalkorDB instances behind TLS termination (FalkorDB Cloud, an AWS NLB TLS listener, Fly.io) could not be reached: the client always opened a plaintext socket and then hung waiting for a RESP reply that never came.

This adds a `FALKORDB_TLS` env var. When set to `true`, the server passes `tls: true` to the underlying redis socket. Certificate and hostname verification stay on (Node defaults SNI to `FALKORDB_HOST`), and there is no plaintext fallback. Any other value, including unset, keeps the existing plaintext behaviour, so current setups are unaffected.

## Changes

- `src/config/index.ts`: parse `FALKORDB_TLS` (strict `'true'` check, same style as `FALKORDB_DEFAULT_READONLY`)
- `src/services/falkordb.service.ts`: spread `tls: true` into the socket options when enabled; log the flag on connect
- `src/services/falkordb.service.test.ts`: new test asserting the TLS socket options
- `README.md`, `.env.example`: document the variable and a "Connecting over TLS" section

## Testing

`npm run lint`, `npm run build`, `npm test` (136 tests) all pass.

Verified live against a self-hosted FalkorDB behind an AWS NLB TLS listener on 6379, driving the built server over stdio with `initialize`, `query_graph`, `query_graph_readonly`, and `list_graphs`:

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| `FALKORDB_TLS` unset, DNS host | hangs, never answers `initialize` (the bug in #80) |
| `FALKORDB_TLS=true`, DNS host | all four calls succeed |
| `FALKORDB_TLS=true`, raw IP host | rejected with `ERR_TLS_CERT_ALTNAME_INVALID` (verification stays on) |

title: [PR] feat(docker): make web UI and MCP server bind address configurable
description:
## Context

**Order of operations, since this spans several commits on #123 before landing here:**

1. #123's first commit ([`f980757`](https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB-MCPServer/commit/f98a0757629defa249006ab149f0b815d43230cd)) switched the Docker default MCP transport to HTTP and published the port without restricting the bind address, with auth as an optional extra (empty `MCP_API_KEY` was allowed). This is what put an unauthenticated-capable listener on the network in the first place.
2. CodeRabbit reviewed that PR while it was open and flagged exactly this, suggesting two separate fixes, either one would have addressed it:

   > "The docker-compose defaults currently start MCP in HTTP mode with an empty API key, which can expose an unauthenticated host-published listener... either require MCP_API_KEY before enabling HTTP or bind the published port to localhost by default."

3. In response, a **follow-up commit pushed to the same #123 branch** — [`9ff305f`](https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB-MCPServer/commit/9ff305f1172e5dd910bcaeb02dc431d2beec5130) ("address review — localhost bind, fixed FalkorDB port, accurate env docs") — is the one that actually closed off network access. It took CodeRabbit's second option, but implemented it by hardcoding `127.0.0.1` with no override anywhere. A third commit on that same PR, [`b2e6d3f`](https://github.com/FalkorDB/FalkorDB-MCPServer/commit/b2e6d3fc60fa3d74ad9b3fe49363033e61199d0), extended the same hardcoded lockdown to the FalkorDB web UI port. All three commits merged together as a single PR, #123.

**Why `9ff305f` was overly aggressive:** CodeRabbit's comment asked for a safe *default*, not for exposure to be made impossible. Hardcoding `127.0.0.1` with no override went further than that: it doesn't just default to a safe state, it removes remote access as a possibility at all, short of hand-editing `docker-compose.yml`. Remote access to FalkorDB (over a LAN, from another machine) is a valid use case, and this PR is what happens when someone actually needs it and finds there's no supported way to get it.

**How this differs from what #123 replaced:** the pre-#123 version was open by default with auth as optional, so reaching the insecure state took no action. This PR keeps the safe default `9ff305f` chose (`127.0.0.1`, unchanged), and only makes it configurable again: exposing either service now requires deliberately setting `MCP_BIND_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0` or `FALKORDB_WEB_BIND_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0` in `.env`.

**Why this isn't just reintroducing the old risk:** binding to localhost by default is a starting value, not enforcement, on its own it doesn't stop someone from opting into `0.0.0.0` without also setting `MCP_API_KEY`, which recreates the exact unauthenticated-listener scenario CodeRabbit flagged. I checked the code: the Bearer-auth check in `src/index.ts` is a silent no-op when `MCP_API_KEY` is empty. So this PR also implements CodeRabbit's other suggested fix, requiring an API key before HTTP i

title: [PR] fix(docker): mount falkordb-data at the real data directory
description:
## Summary

The `falkordb-data` volume mounts at `/data`, but that's not where FalkorDB actually writes anything.

The image's `run.sh` (`/var/lib/falkordb/bin/run.sh`) execs `redis-server` with `--dir "${FALKORDB_DATA_PATH}"`, and the image sets `FALKORDB_DATA_PATH=/var/lib/falkordb/data`. Docker mounts volumes at the literal container path and does not follow symlinks, so `falkordb-data:/data` never received a single write. I confirmed this directly: `redis-cli config get dir` inside a running container returns `/var/lib/falkordb/data`, while `docker inspect` shows the volume mounted at `/data`, two separate paths. Every RDB snapshot was landing in the container's writable layer, not the volume, so all graph data was lost on `docker compose down`, `--force-recreate`, or an image upgrade, even though the volume looked correctly configured.

Fix: mount the volume at the real path, `/var/lib/falkordb/data`.

@galshubeli caught and confirmed the actual bug, and correctly pointed out that `/data` is not itself a symlink. It's a real directory that *contains* a symlink `data -> /var/lib/falkordb/data`, because the upstream Dockerfile runs `mkdir -p /data` and then `ln -s`, so the link lands inside. That doesn't change the conclusion. Thank you for the sharper description and for splitting this from the snapshot-cadence change below.

## Splitting this PR

Per review feedback, this PR is now the mount fix only. The `FALKORDB_SAVE` / `--save` cadence change from the original version has been dropped rather than fixed up, in favor of a general `REDIS_ARGS` pass-through in a follow-up PR, since:

- Redis already saves on `SIGTERM` whenever save points are configured (`finishShutdown()` in `server.c` runs a synchronous `rdbSave` before exit when `saveparamslen > 0`), and the image ships Redis's built-in save points by default. So a normal `docker compose down` already persists once this mount fix lands — the cadence was never load-bearing for #177.
- The reviewer's off-switch fix (`FALKORDB_SAVE-` instead of `FALKORDB_SAVE:-`) would still have disabled the shutdown save along with the periodic one, since both are gated on the same `saveparamslen` count.
- A general pass-through lets anyone set `--appendonly yes`, tune `--save`, or anything else `redis-server` supports, through the mechanism FalkorDB's own docs already document, with no new variable to validate.

## Two things worth knowing on upgrade

- **Existing volumes get a harmless symlink loop.** A `falkordb-data` volume created under the old `/data` mount holds the image's `data -> /var/lib/falkordb/data` entry. Remounted at the new path, that becomes `/var/lib/falkordb/data/data -> /var/lib/falkordb/data`. Confirmed this reproduces exactly, and that the container starts and serves normally regardless. No graph data is lost either way, since the old layout never persisted any. Running `docker compose down && docker volume rm falkordb-data` clears it, but is not required.

title: [PR] feat(docker): pass REDIS_ARGS through to redis-server
description:
## Summary

Split off from #174 per review feedback from @galshubeli.

The compose entrypoint built `REDIS_ARGS` from scratch, using it only to carry the auth flags derived from `FALKORDB_USERNAME`/`FALKORDB_PASSWORD`. There was no supported way to hand `redis-server` any other flag — `--appendonly`, a custom `--save` policy, anything else the image's `run.sh` accepts via `REDIS_ARGS`.

This adds a `REDIS_ARGS` compose variable that passes through from `.env`, and appends the auth flags to whatever the user supplied instead of overwriting it.

## Why not the original `FALKORDB_SAVE` approach

The original version of #174 added a `FALKORDB_SAVE` variable (default `60 1`) injected into `REDIS_ARGS` to tighten the RDB snapshot cadence. @galshubeli found six issues with it, one of which could leave the whole stack crash-looping on a malformed value. Rather than patch each one, this PR drops the variable entirely in favor of a general pass-through:

- No new variable to validate — `REDIS_ARGS` is handed to `redis-server` exactly as `run.sh` already does for every other deployment of this image.
- No default cadence change — Redis's built-in save points (`3600 1 300 100 60 10000`) are untouched. They already persist, and Redis's `SIGTERM` handler does a synchronous save before exit whenever save points are configured, so a plain `docker compose down` already persists cleanly once #174 lands.
- No off-switch footgun — the original design's off switch (`FALKORDB_SAVE=`) would have also disabled the shutdown save, not just the periodic one, since both are gated on the same save-point count. There's no such footgun here since nothing sets `--save` by default.
- Anyone who wants tighter snapshots, AOF durability, or anything else, sets it themselves: `REDIS_ARGS=--appendonly yes` or `REDIS_ARGS=--save 60 1`, through the mechanism FalkorDB's own docs already document.

## Regression this specifically fixes

On `main` today, `REDIS_ARGS` isn't passed into the container at all, so this isn't a live regression — but it's exactly the failure mode called out in review: a user who set `REDIS_ARGS` for AOF and also has a password configured needs both to take effect together. Verified directly:

| `REDIS_ARGS` | password | ACL username | effective config |
|---|---|---|---|
| unset | unset | — | `appendonly no`, no auth (identical to today) |
| `--appendonly yes` | unset | — | `appendonly yes`, no auth |
| unset | set | — | `appendonly no`, `requirepass` set |
| `--appendonly yes` | set | — | `appendonly yes` **and** `requirepass` set |
| `--appendonly yes` | set | `alice` | `appendonly yes`, `requirepass` set, ACL user `alice` created |

All five read back from a running container via `redis-cli config get` / `acl list`.

## Escaping

The `$$` -> `$` accounting in the compose `command:` script is easy to get backwards. Rather than trust `docker compose config` (which re-escapes its own output and would silently hide a mistake here), I created the container without

title: [Issue] MCP HTTP transport binds all interfaces outside Docker Compose, with auth optional
description:
## Context

#175 added \`MCP_BIND_ADDRESS\` and a startup guard that refuses to run the MCP server when it's published on a non-local address without \`MCP_API_KEY\` set. That guard, and the whole \`MCP_BIND_ADDRESS\` variable, only affects **what interface the Docker Compose published port binds to** (\`docker-compose.yml\`'s \`ports:\` mapping). It does not change what the server itself listens on.

\`startHTTPServer()\` calls \`httpServer.listen(port, cb)\` with no host argument (\`src/index.ts\`), so the Node process always binds all interfaces (\`::\`/\`0.0.0.0\`). Inside a container this is required — binding loopback there would break Compose's published-port forwarding entirely — but it means the guard only protects the one deployment shape (Docker Compose) that happens to also publish a host-bound port in front of it.

Anything that reaches the container's HTTP port directly bypasses the guard and \`MCP_BIND_ADDRESS\` entirely:
- \`docker run -p 0.0.0.0:8080:8080 falkordb/mcpserver:latest\` with no \`MCP_API_KEY\`
- a Kubernetes \`Service\`/\`Ingress\` in front of the container
- bare-metal \`npm start\` / \`node dist/index.js\` on a host with a routable interface

In all of these, \`config.mcp.apiKey\` empty means the Bearer check at \`src/index.ts\` (inside the request handler) is a silent no-op — the exact unauthenticated-HTTP-on-the-network scenario #175's guard was meant to prevent, just reached through a path the guard doesn't cover.

## Proposed fix

Introduce a real listen-address setting (e.g. \`MCP_HOST\`, defaulting to \`0.0.0.0\` to preserve current container behavior) that \`startHTTPServer()\` actually passes to \`listen()\`, and extend \`enforceLocalBindWithoutApiKey()\` (or an equivalent check) to key off that value when \`MCP_BIND_ADDRESS\` isn't set — so the guard applies to every deployment shape, not just Compose.

This is a breaking change to the published image's default posture: it would mean \`docker run -p 3000:8080 falkordb/mcpserver:latest\` (documented in README.md's Docker quickstart) refuses to start without a key, and README.md's several "MCP_API_KEY ... (optional)" statements would need to become conditional. That's why it wasn't folded into #175 — flagging it as tracked follow-up instead.

cc @galshubeli, who raised the underlying gap during #175's review.

title: [PR] Fix stdio protocol corruption by redirecting console methods to stderr
description:
In stdio transport mode, any output to stdout (console.log, console.warn, etc.) corrupts the MCP JSON-RPC protocol stream, causing immediate client disconnection.

## Changes

- **src/index.ts**: Added `redirectConsoleToStderr()` function that monkey-patches all console methods to write to stderr when stdio transport is active
- **src/services/logger.service.ts**: Changed console.warn to console.error for log directory creation failures
- **src/stdio-console.test.ts**: Added test suite verifying console redirection prevents stdout pollution

## Implementation

The fix activates automatically when the server starts in stdio mode:

```typescript
async function startStdioServer(): Promise<void> {
  // Redirect console to stderr to prevent corruption of the MCP protocol stream
  redirectConsoleToStderr();
  
  const transport = new StdioServerTransport();
  await server.connect(transport);
}

function redirectConsoleToStderr(): void {
  console.log = (...args: unknown[]) => {
    process.stderr.write(`[LOG] ${args.map(String).join(' ')}\n`);
  };
  // ... same for warn, info, debug, error
}
```

HTTP transport is unaffected as it doesn't use stdio for protocol communication.

title: [Issue] FalkorDB data is not actually persisted across container recreation
description:
`docker-compose.yml` mounts the `falkordb-data` volume at `/data`, but FalkorDB's `redis-server` writes to `/var/lib/falkordb/data`. `/data` is only a symlink to that path inside the image, and Docker mounts volumes at the literal container path without following symlinks, so every write lands in the container's ephemeral layer instead of the volume. All graph data is silently lost on `docker compose down`, `--force-recreate`, or an image upgrade, even though the volume looks correctly configured.

Confirmed directly: `stat`/`mount` inside a running container show `/data` and `/var/lib/falkordb/data` as two separate mounts.

Fixed by #174, which also tightens the default snapshot cadence for local dev via a new `FALKORDB_SAVE` var.

Related: #176 (port default), #178 (bind-address configurability).

cc @gkorland @barakb

title: [Issue] No supported way to expose FalkorDB web UI or MCP server beyond localhost
description:
#123 hardcoded both the web UI and MCP server published ports to bind `127.0.0.1`, with no override. That's the right default, but there's currently no supported way to reach either service from another machine (e.g. over a LAN) without hand-editing `docker-compose.yml`. Setting `FALKORDB_WEB_PORT`/`MCP_PORT` in `.env` isn't enough, since the bind address, not just the port, is what's blocking remote access.

Fixed by #175, which adds `FALKORDB_WEB_BIND_ADDRESS`/`MCP_BIND_ADDRESS` (both default to `127.0.0.1`, no behavior change unless set), plus a startup guard that refuses to run the MCP server on a non-local bind without `MCP_API_KEY` set.

Related: #176 (port default), #177 (persistence).

cc @gkorland @barakb

title: [PR] chore(deps): ignore TypeScript 7.0.x in Dependabot
description:
## What

Adds a Dependabot `ignore` rule for the `typescript` **7.0.x** line (npm ecosystem). Scoped to 7.0.x only — **7.1+ is intentionally allowed**.

## Why

TypeScript 7.0 is the new native (Go) compiler rewrite. It ships no JavaScript **Compiler API** at the package root, and its peer range is rejected by `@typescript-eslint` / `ts-node`. Bumping `typescript` to 7.0.x therefore fails the install with an `npm ERESOLVE` conflict:

```
npm error While resolving: @typescript-eslint/eslint-plugin@8.63.0
npm error Found: typescript@7.0.2
npm error Conflicting peer dependency: typescript@6.0.3
npm error   peer typescript@">=4.8.4 <6.1.0" from @typescript-eslint/eslint-plugin@8.63.0
```

This is exactly what breaks **#144** (Dependabot `typescript 6.0.3 → 7.0.2`), failing the `Test & Build` jobs.

## Why 7.0.x only (not 7.x)

**TypeScript 7.1** is expected to restore the programmatic JS Compiler API. Scoping the ignore to `7.0.x` lets Dependabot propose **7.1+** once it lands (CI will then verify compatibility), rather than blocking the entire major line. 6.x patch/minor updates are unaffected.

Note: #144 can be closed once this merges — Dependabot will stop re-proposing the 7.0.x bump.

title: [Issue] Expose query parameters in the query_graph tool
description:
## Summary

The `query_graph` MCP tool does not expose a way to pass query parameters. The underlying `falkorDBService.executeQuery(graphName, query, params?, readOnly?)` already accepts a `params` argument, but the tool handler hardcodes `undefined`, so callers cannot use parameterized Cypher queries.

## Problem

Without parameter support, an AI model (or any MCP client) driving the tool must string-concatenate values directly into the Cypher query text. This is:

- **Unsafe** — it's a query-injection vector, the same class of problem as SQL injection.
- **Brittle** — the model has to handle escaping, quoting, and type coercion by hand, which frequently produces malformed queries.

Parameterized queries (`$name` placeholders) are the correct, idiomatic way to inject values into Cypher.

## Proposed change

Add an optional `params` field to the `query_graph` tool input schema and wire it through to `executeQuery`:

```ts
params: z.record(z.string(), z.any()).optional()
  .describe("Optional query parameters, referenced in the query as $name. Note: FalkorDB does not allow parameters in LIMIT/SKIP clauses."),
```

```ts
const { graphName, query, params, readOnly } = z.object(queryGraphSchema).parse(args);
// ...
const result = await falkorDBService.executeQuery(graphName, query, params, isReadOnly);
```

## Notes

- The schema description should document the FalkorDB limitation that parameters are not allowed in `LIMIT`/`SKIP` clauses, to save the model from a confusing failure.
- This is a public API change to a documented MCP tool, so `README.md` should be updated with a usage example.
